results.title: Conductor ideal of a subalgebra
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $S$ a commutative $R$-algebra and $A$ an $R$-subalgebra of $S$. The conductor ideal of $A$ is the ideal of $S$ consisting of all $s \in S$ such that $st \in A$ for every $t \in S$; it is the largest ideal of $S$ contained in $A$.

results.title: Membership in the conductor ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ and $S$ be commutative semirings with $S$ an $R$-algebra, and let $A$ be an $R$-subalgebra of $S$. An element $s \in S$ lies in the conductor ideal of $A$ if and only if $st \in A$ for every $t \in S$.

results.title: Universal property of the conductor ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ and $S$ be commutative semirings with $S$ an $R$-algebra, let $A$ be an $R$-subalgebra of $S$, and let $I$ be an ideal of $S$. Then $I$ is contained in the conductor ideal of $A$ if and only if $I$ is contained in $A$.

results.title: The conductor ideal lies in the subalgebra
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $S$ a commutative $R$-algebra and $A$ an $R$-subalgebra of $S$. Then the conductor ideal of $A$ is contained in $A$.

results.title: Monotonicity of the conductor ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $S$ a commutative $R$-algebra and $A \subseteq B$ two $R$-subalgebras of $S$. Then the conductor ideal of $A$ is contained in the conductor ideal of $B$.

results.title: Conductor ideal of the whole algebra
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring and $S$ a commutative $R$-algebra. The conductor ideal of $S$, viewed as an $R$-subalgebra of itself, is the unit ideal $S$.

results.title: The conductor ideal is the unit ideal only for the whole algebra
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $S$ a commutative $R$-algebra and $A$ an $R$-subalgebra of $S$. The conductor ideal of $A$ is all of $S$ if and only if $A = S$.

results.title: Preimage of a conductor ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, $S$ and $T$ commutative $R$-algebras, $f \colon S \to T$ a homomorphism of $R$-algebras and $B$ an $R$-subalgebra of $T$. Then the preimage under $f$ of the conductor ideal of $B$ is contained in the conductor ideal of the subalgebra $f^{-1}(B)$ of $S$.

results.title: Conductor of a monogenic subalgebra
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $S$ a commutative $R$-algebra and $x \in S$. The conductor ideal of the subalgebra $R[x]$ of $S$ generated by $x$ equals the conductor of $x$, the ideal of all $a \in S$ such that $ab \in R[x]$ for every $b \in S$.

results.title: A finite overring has nonzero conductor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K$, and let $T$ be an $R$-subalgebra of $K$ that is finitely generated as an $R$-module. Then the conductor ideal of the image of $R$ in $T$ (the smallest $R$-subalgebra of $T$) is nonzero.

results.title: A subalgebra of a field with nonzero conductor is finite
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, $K$ a field that is an $R$-algebra, and $T$ an $R$-subalgebra of $K$. If the conductor ideal of the image of $R$ in $T$ (the smallest $R$-subalgebra of $T$) is nonzero, then $T$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module.

results.title: Finiteness of an overring via its conductor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Noetherian integral domain with fraction field $K$, and let $T$ be an $R$-subalgebra of $K$. Then the conductor ideal of the image of $R$ in $T$ (the smallest $R$-subalgebra of $T$) is nonzero if and only if $T$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module.

results.title: Finiteness of the integral closure via the conductor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a Noetherian integral domain with fraction field $K$, and let $\overline{R}$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $K$, viewed as an $R$-algebra. The conductor ideal of the smallest $R$-subalgebra of $\overline{R}$ (the image of $R$) is a nonzero ideal of $\overline{R}$ if and only if $\overline{R}$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module.

results.title: Prime ideals stay prime under denominator clearing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $O$ and $B$ be commutative rings, let $B$ be an $O$-algebra whose structure map $f \colon O \to B$ is injective, let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal of $O$, and let $\mathfrak c$ be an ideal of $O$ with $\mathfrak c + \mathfrak p = O$ such that $f(x)\,b$ lies in the image of $f$ for every $x \in \mathfrak c$ and every $b \in B$. Then the ideal $\mathfrak p B$ of $B$ generated by $f(\mathfrak p)$ is prime.

Then the ideal $\mathfrak p B$ of $B$ generated by $f(\mathfrak p)$ is maximal.

results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: Contraction after extension is the identity on primes not containing `𝔠`.

results.title: Contraction of a nonzero ideal is nonzero
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: Contraction of a nonzero ideal is nonzero when `𝔠` is nonzero: a nonzero element of `𝔠` clears a nonzero element of `𝔮` back to a nonzero element of the contraction.

results.title: Extension after contraction fixes primes away from the conductor
results.caption: Lemma

results.title: Bijection of primes away from the conductor
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Bijection of nonzero primes away from the conductor

results.title: Büchi sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a natural number. A sequence of integers $u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ is a Büchi sequence of length $M$ when the second differences of its squares equal $2$ along its first $M$ terms, that is, $u_{j+2}^2 - 2u_{j+1}^2 + u_j^2 = 2$ for every $j$ with $j + 2 < M$.

results.title: Trivial sequences in Büchi's problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a natural number. A sequence of integers $u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ is trivial at length $M$ when there is an integer $x$ with $u_j^2 = (x + j)^2$ for every $j < M$; equivalently, after changing the signs of some of its terms, its first $M$ terms are the consecutive integers $x, x + 1, \dots, x + M - 1$.

results.title: Büchi's square-sequence conjecture
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: There is a natural number $M \ge 5$ such that every integer Büchi sequence of length $M$ is trivial: for every sequence of integers $u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ with $u_{j+2}^2 - 2u_{j+1}^2 + u_j^2 = 2$ for all $j$ with $j + 2 < M$, there is an integer $x$ with $u_j^2 = (x + j)^2$ for all $j < M$.

results.title: Resolution of Büchi's square-sequence conjecture
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a natural number $M \ge 5$ such that every integer Büchi sequence of length $M$ is trivial: for every sequence of integers $u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ with $u_{j+2}^2 - 2u_{j+1}^2 + u_j^2 = 2$ for all $j$ with $j + 2 < M$, there is an integer $x$ with $u_j^2 = (x + j)^2$ for all $j < M$.

results.title: First term of a compound sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and all sequences $a$, $b$ of natural numbers, the compound sequence $c$ of $a$ and $b$ satisfies $c_0 = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$.

results.title: Last term of a compound sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and all sequences $a$, $b$ of natural numbers, the compound sequence $c$ of $a$ and $b$ satisfies $c_n = b_1 b_2 \cdots b_n$.

results.title: Brauer–Shockley formula for the Frobenius number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A_1, \dots, A_k$ be positive integers with $\gcd(A_1, \dots, A_k) = 1$, let $S$ be the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ they generate, and let $a = A_i$ be one of them with $a \ge 2$. For $1 \le x \le a - 1$ let $m_x$ be the least element of $S$ congruent to $x$ modulo $a$. If $M$ is the largest of the numbers $m_x$, then $M - a$ is the largest integer not in $S$, that is, the Frobenius number of $S$.

results.title: Riesz–Schauder theorem, kernel part
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T : E \to E$ be a compact bounded linear operator, let $\mu \neq 0$ be a scalar and let $I$ be the identity of $E$. Then the kernel of $\mu I - T$ is finite-dimensional.

results.title: Continuous projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and let $K$ be a finite-dimensional subspace of $E$. Then there is a continuous linear map $P : E \to E$ such that $P x = x$ for every $x \in K$ and $P x \in K$ for every $x \in E$.

results.title: Riesz–Schauder theorem, range part
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T : E \to E$ be a compact bounded linear operator, let $\mu \neq 0$ be a scalar and let $I$ be the identity of $E$. Then the range of $\mu I - T$ is closed in $E$.

results.title: Fredholm alternative, Riesz–Schauder form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T : E \to E$ be a compact bounded linear operator, let $\mu \neq 0$ be a scalar and let $I$ be the identity of $E$. Then either $\mu I - T$ is bijective, or the kernel of $\mu I - T$ is nonzero and finite-dimensional and the range of $\mu I - T$ is closed.

results.title: Riesz–Schauder theorem on a Hilbert space
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a compact operator on $E$, let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ with $\mu \ne 0$, and let $I$ be the identity operator on $E$. Then the range of $\mu I - T$ is the orthogonal complement of the kernel of its adjoint: $\operatorname{ran}(\mu I - T) = \ker\big((\mu I - T)^*\big)^\perp$.

results.title: Adjoint of a shifted operator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on $E$ with adjoint $T^*$, let $\mu \in \mathbb{K}$ and let $I$ be the identity operator on $E$. Then $(\mu I - T)^* = \overline{\mu} I - T^*$, where $\overline{\mu}$ is the complex conjugate of $\mu$ (so $\overline{\mu} = \mu$ when $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$).

results.title: Standardized laws with finite third moment
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a standardized law when it is a probability measure with mean $\int x \, d\mu(x) = 0$ and variance $1$, and has finite third absolute moment $\int |x|^3 \, d\mu(x) < \infty$.

results.title: I.i.d. product law
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the i.i.d. product law of $\mu$ is the measure on the sequence space $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ that is the infinite product $\mu^{\otimes \mathbb{N}}$ of countably many copies of $\mu$ when $\mu$ is a probability measure, and the zero measure otherwise.

results.title: Normalized sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a positive integer $n$ and a real sequence $\omega = (\omega_0, \omega_1, \dots)$, the normalized sum $S_n(\omega)$ is the sum of the first $n$ coordinates divided by $\sqrt{n}$: $S_n(\omega) = (\omega_0 + \dots + \omega_{n-1})/\sqrt{n}$.

results.title: Law of the normalized sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and a positive integer $n$, the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$ is the pushforward of the i.i.d. law of $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ (the product measure $\mu^{\otimes \mathbb{N}}$ when $\mu$ is a probability measure, and the zero measure otherwise) under the normalized sum $\omega \mapsto (\omega_0 + \dots + \omega_{n-1})/\sqrt{n}$.

results.title: Standard normal CDF
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $\Phi(x)$ is the value at $x$ of the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, that is, the probability that a standard normal random variable is at most $x$.

results.title: Third absolute moment
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The third absolute moment of a measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is the real number $\int |x|^3 \, d\mu(x)$, taken to be $0$ when $x \mapsto |x|^3$ is not integrable with respect to $\mu$.

results.title: Finite third absolute moment as an $L^3$ condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the identity function $x \mapsto x$ belongs to $L^3(\mu)$ if and only if the function $x \mapsto |x|^3$ is $\mu$-integrable.

results.summary: If $\mu$ is a standardized law on $\mathbb{R}$, then the i.i.d. product law of $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is a probability measure.

results.title: Measurability of the normalized sum

results.title: The normalized law is a probability measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every standardized law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (a probability measure with mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment) and every positive integer $n$, the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$ is a probability measure.

results.title: Coordinates of the i.i.d. product are independent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $\mu$ is a standardized law on $\mathbb{R}$, then the coordinate maps $\omega \mapsto \omega_i$ on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$, for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, are mutually independent under the i.i.d. product law of $\mu$.

results.title: Coordinate laws of the i.i.d. product

results.summary: If $\mu$ is a standardized law on $\mathbb{R}$ and $i$ is a natural number, then the pushforward of the i.i.d. product law of $\mu$ under the coordinate map $\omega \mapsto \omega_i$ from $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is $\mu$.

results.title: Standardized laws have an integrable third absolute moment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $\mu$ is a standardized law on $\mathbb{R}$, then the function $x \mapsto |x|^3$ is integrable with respect to $\mu$.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the third absolute moment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the third absolute moment $\int_{\mathbb{R}} |x|^3 \, d\mu(x)$ is nonnegative.

results.title: The third absolute moment of a standardized law is positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $\mu$ is a standardized law on $\mathbb{R}$, that is, a probability measure with mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment, then its third absolute moment $\int |x|^3 \, d\mu(x)$ is strictly positive.

results.title: The CDF error is at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$, $n$ a positive integer and $x$ a real number. Let $F_{\mu,n}$ be the distribution function of the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$ and $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function. Then $|F_{\mu,n}(x) - \Phi(x)| \le 1$.

results.title: The CDF errors are bounded above
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$, let $n$ be a positive integer, let $F$ be the cumulative distribution function of the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$, and let $\Phi$ be the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Then the set $\{|F(x) - \Phi(x)| : x \in \mathbb{R}\}$ is bounded above.

results.title: Each CDF error is at most the Kolmogorov error
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$, $n$ a positive integer, $F_{\mu,n}$ the distribution function of the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$ and $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function. Then for every real $x$, $|F_{\mu,n}(x) - \Phi(x)| \le \sup_{y \in \mathbb{R}} |F_{\mu,n}(y) - \Phi(y)|$, the right side being the Kolmogorov error of $\mu$ at $n$.

results.title: The Kolmogorov error is nonnegative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every positive integer $n$, the Kolmogorov error of $\mu$ at $n$, that is $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |F_{\mu,n}(x) - \Phi(x)|$ where $F_{\mu,n}$ is Mathlib's cumulative distribution function of the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, is nonnegative.

results.title: The Kolmogorov error is at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every positive integer $n$, the Kolmogorov error of $\mu$ at $n$, that is $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |F_{\mu,n}(x) - \Phi(x)|$ where $F_{\mu,n}$ is Mathlib's cumulative distribution function of the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, is at most $1$.

results.title: Kolmogorov error bounds are uniform CDF bounds
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}$, let $n$ be a positive integer, let $F$ be the cumulative distribution function of the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n$, and let $\Phi$ be the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Then for every real $a$, the Kolmogorov error of $\mu$ at $n$ is at most $a$ if and only if $|F(x) - \Phi(x)| \le a$ for every real $x$.

results.title: The standard Gaussian is a standardized law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The standard normal law $N(0,1)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a standardized law: it is a probability measure with mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment.

results.title: The normalized law with one summand
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every standardized law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (a probability measure with mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment), the normalized law of $\mu$ at $n = 1$ is $\mu$ itself.

results.title: The Kolmogorov error vanishes for one standard Gaussian summand
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be the distribution function of the normalized law of the standard normal law $N(0,1)$ at $n = 1$, and $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function. Then the Kolmogorov error of $N(0,1)$ at $n = 1$, $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |F(x) - \Phi(x)|$, equals $0$.

results.title: Standardized i.i.d. models
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a measurable space with a measure $P$, and let $(X_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be real-valued functions on $\Omega$. They form a standardized i.i.d. model when $P$ is a probability measure, every $X_i$ is measurable, the $X_i$ are mutually independent under $P$, every $X_i$ has the same law under $P$ as $X_0$, and $X_0$ has mean $\int_\Omega X_0 \, dP = 0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment…

results.title: The common law of an i.i.d. model is standardized
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$ and $X_0, X_1, \dots$ real-valued functions on $\Omega$ forming an i.i.d. model: $P$ is a probability measure, the $X_i$ are measurable, independent and identically distributed, and $X_0$ has mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment. Then the law of $X_0$, the pushforward of $P$ under $X_0$, is a standardized law.

results.title: The joint law of a standardized i.i.d. model
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $(X_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a standardized i.i.d. model on a measurable space $\Omega$ with measure $P$, then the law under $P$ of the sequence map $\omega \mapsto (X_i(\omega))_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ equals the i.i.d. product law of the law of $X_0$ under $P$.

results.title: Normalized sums of an i.i.d. model have the canonical law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a probability measure on a measurable space $\Omega$ and let $X_0, X_1, \dots$ be real random variables on $\Omega$ that are measurable, independent and identically distributed under $P$, with $X_0$ of mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment. Then for every positive integer $n$, the law under $P$ of $(X_0 + \dots + X_{n-1})/\sqrt{n}$ equals the normalized law at $n$ of the law of $X_0$.

results.title: Third absolute moment of the common law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a measure on a measurable space $\Omega$ and $X_0, X_1, \dots$ real-valued functions on $\Omega$ forming an i.i.d. model: $P$ is a probability measure, the $X_i$ are measurable, independent and identically distributed, and $X_0$ has mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite third absolute moment. Then the third absolute moment of the law of $X_0$ equals $\int_\Omega |X_0(\omega)|^3 \, dP(\omega)$.
